cmimc-2020-combinatorics-01.title: Follow the forced games
cmimc-2020-combinatorics-01.body:
Daniel has played $4$ games against $4$ different opponents, so he has played everyone: Albert, Bassim, Clara and Eugene. That is Albert's only game. Clara has played $3$ games with distinct opponents, none of them Albert: so she played Bassim, Daniel and Eugene. Now Bassim has played Daniel and Clara: $2$ games, as required. Eugene has played Daniel and Clara: $2$ games.

**Answer: 2**

cmimc-2020-combinatorics-01.title: Degree sum
cmimc-2020-combinatorics-01.body:
Treat games as edges of a graph. The degrees are $1,2,3,4,e$ and the sum must be even, so $e$ is even: $e\in\{0,2,4\}$. Daniel (degree $4$) is adjacent to everybody, so $e\ge1$, and Albert's single game is with Daniel. Eugene cannot have $4$ games because he cannot play Albert. So $e=2$.

**Answer: 2**

cmimc-2020-combinatorics-02.title: Count by matching the True answers
cmimc-2020-combinatorics-02.body:
Say the correct answers are $5$ True and $4$ False. All $\binom95=126$ ways of choosing which $5$ answers David marks True are equally likely. Suppose he marks $k$ of the $5$ truly-True questions as True. Then he uses $5-k$ of his True marks on the $4$ truly-False questions, so he answers $4-(5-k)=k-1$ of those correctly as False. Total correct: $k+(k-1)=2k-1$. This is at least $5$ iff $k\ge3$.

Number of ways for given $k$: $\binom5k\binom4{5-k}=\binom5k\binom4{k-1}$. So the favourable count is

$$\binom53\binom42+\binom54\binom43+\binom55\binom44=60+20+1=81,$$

and the probability is $\frac{81}{126}=\frac9{14}$.

**Answer: $\frac{9}{14}$**

cmimc-2020-combinatorics-03.title: Reflections of a circle of positions
cmimc-2020-combinatorics-03.body:
Read the array positions $1,\dots,10$ as the positions around a circle (indices mod $10$). The action with parameter $n$ sends the entry in position $j$ to position $n+1-j \pmod{10}$: indeed the first block is reversed ($j\mapsto n+1-j$) and the second block is reversed ($j\mapsto 10+n+1-j\equiv n+1-j$). So each action is a reflection of the $10$-gon, and $n=1,\dots,10$ give all $10$ reflections.

The composition of two reflections $j\mapsto a+1-j$ and $j\mapsto b+1-j$ is the rotation $j\mapsto j+(a-b)$. So the arrangements reachable are exactly those obtained from $1,2,\dots,10$ by an element of the dihedral group of the $10$-gon: $10$ rotations and $10$ reflections. Since the entries are distinct and $10\ge3$, all $20$ resulting arrays are different.

(A breadth-first search over all reachable arrays also finds exactly $20$.)

**Answer: 20**

cmimc-2020-combinatorics-04.title: Corners and a snake
cmimc-2020-combinatorics-04.body:
Walls are unit segments, and two walls may not even share an endpoint. The triangular grid has $1+2+\dots+10=55$ lattice points, and each wall uses $2$ of them, no point used twice. So there are at most $\lfloor55/2\rfloor=27$ walls.

*Construction.* Number the rows of points $0,\dots,9$ from the top (row $r$ has $r+1$ points). Walk along row $0$, go down to row $1$ and walk it right to left, go down to row $2$ and walk it left to right, and so on, alternating. This is a path through all $55$ points using $54$ grid segments. Make walls out of the 1st, 3rd, 5th, ..., 53rd segments: $27$ walls, no two sharing a point. Each wall is a side of some unit triangle; two different walls cannot belong to the same triangle (two sides of a triangle share a corner), so every wall can be assigned to a different country.

**Answer: 27**

cmimc-2020-combinatorics-05.title: Last of 3 and 6 to be picked
cmimc-2020-combinatorics-05.body:
Cards $3$ and $6$ keep their relative order (3 above 6) until one of them is picked. The relative order of $3$ and $6$ at the end is decided by whichever of them was picked last: it sits above the other.

- *Neither is ever picked.* Then at every step the top card is neither $3$ nor $6$, so $4$ of the $6$ eligible cards are neither; the probability is $(4/6)^{10}=(2/3)^{10}$. Then $3$ is above $6$: failure.
- *At least one is picked.* A history is a sequence of $10$ picks (each pick avoids the current top card). Swapping the labels $3\leftrightarrow6$ in every pick maps histories to histories (the top card is always the last pick, so legality is preserved) with the same probability $6^{-10}$, and exchanges "last pick among $\{3,6\}$ is $6$" with "is $3$". So by symmetry the probability that $6$ was picked last is $\frac12$.

Thus the answer is

$$\frac12\left(1-\Big(\frac23\Big)^{10}\right)=\frac{3^{10}-2^{10}}{2\cdot3^{10}}=\frac{58025}{118098}.$$

(An exact computation over all $6^{10}$-weighted states gives the same fraction.)

**Answer: $\frac{3^{10}-2^{10}}{2\cdot3^{10}}=\frac{58025}{118098}$**

cmimc-2020-combinatorics-06.title: Every island needs 3 bridges
cmimc-2020-combinatorics-06.body:
A tour is a Hamiltonian cycle on the surviving islands, so each surviving island uses two different bridges.

*Lower bound.* Suppose an island $I$ had at most $2$ bridges. If it has $\le1$, then any eruption elsewhere leaves $I$ without two bridges. If it has exactly $2$, erupt a neighbour: $I$ is left with one bridge. Either way no tour exists. So every island has at least $3$ bridges, the total number of bridge ends is at least $24$, and there are at least $12$ bridges.

*Construction with 12 bridges.* Label the islands $0,\dots,7$ and build the bridges $i$--$(i+1)$ (mod $8$) and $i$--$(i+4)$: the $8$-cycle plus the four diagonals joining opposite islands (a cubic graph with $12$ edges). The graph is symmetric under rotating the labels, so it suffices to check that removing island $0$ leaves a Hamiltonian cycle: $1\to5\to4\to3\to7\to6\to2\to1$ uses the bridges $1$-$5$, $5$-$4$, $4$-$3$, $3$-$7$, $7$-$6$, $6$-$2$, $2$-$1$, all present. Rotating this cycle handles every other eruption.

**Answer: 12**

cmimc-2020-combinatorics-07.title: Marked edges form two cliques
cmimc-2020-combinatorics-07.body:
Call two vertices *friends* if the edge between them is marked (and every vertex is its own friend). If $uv$ and $vw$ are marked, the triangle $uvw$ already has at least $2$ marked edges, so it must have all $3$: $uw$ is marked. So friendship is an equivalence relation. If there were three classes, one vertex from each would form a triangle with no marked edge, which is not allowed. So there are at most $2$ classes, and the marked edges are exactly the pairs inside the classes.

If the classes have sizes $a$ and $2020-a$, the number of marked edges is $\binom a2+\binom{2020-a}2$, which by convexity is smallest for $a=1010$: $2\binom{1010}2=1010\cdot1009=1019090$. (One class would give $\binom{2020}2$, which is larger.)

This works: a triangle inside a class has $3$ marked edges, and a triangle with vertices in both classes has exactly $1$.

**Answer: 1019090**

cmimc-2020-combinatorics-08.title: Pairs of columns and a transfer recurrence
cmimc-2020-combinatorics-08.body:
*Setup.* Two mooncakes are adjacent when their circles touch (same column neighbours, or cakes in neighbouring columns offset by half a cake). Each of the $100$ columns has $3$ mooncakes. Whenever she takes a mooncake, all adjacent ones are destroyed, so we want a maximum independent set.

*Maximum.* Group columns into $50$ pairs $(1,2),(3,4),\dots$. In a pair the $6$ cakes split into two triangles of mutually touching cakes, so at most $1$ cake can be taken from each: at most $2$ per pair, at most $100$ overall. This is achieved by taking the top and bottom cakes of every odd column. So $M=100$, and a selection of $100$ cakes is exactly one that takes $2$ cakes from every pair.

*Counting.* A pair has $6$ possible patterns of $2$ non-touching cakes: both in the odd column (top and bottom), both in the even column (top and bottom), or one cake in each column ($4$ non-touching combinations). Between consecutive pairs only the even column of one pair touches the odd column of the next, which restricts which patterns can follow each other. Let $f_n$ be the number of valid selections with $n$ pairs. Tracking the six patterns with these touching rules (a transfer-matrix recursion) gives a closed form

$$f_n=F_{2n+4}+\binom n2-2 .$$

For $n=1$ this gives $F_6+0-2=6$, as expected (the six patterns). A direct dynamic programme over the columns gives $f_n=6,20,56,148,385$ for $n=1,\dots,5$, matching the formula. For $n=50$ pairs: $f_{50}=F_{104}+\binom{50}2-2=F_{104}+1223$, and the same programme on all $100$ columns gives $2427893228399975083676$.

**Answer: $(M,n)=(100,\ F_{104}+1223)$**

cmimc-2020-combinatorics-09.title: Count eventually periodic sequences
cmimc-2020-combinatorics-09.body:
A string in $\Gamma$ is determined by its length, so $F_D$ corresponds to the $0/1$ sequence $s_t=[\delta^t(q_0)\in F]$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$. The maximum size of a diverse set is the number of distinct sequences that arise.

The orbit $q_0,\delta(q_0),\dots$ is a tail of $\mu$ states followed by a cycle of $\lambda$ states with $\mu+\lambda\le6$, so $s$ is eventually periodic with preperiod $\le\mu$ and period $\le\lambda$. Hence its *minimal* preperiod $\mu'$ and minimal period $\lambda'$ satisfy $\mu'+\lambda'\le6$. Conversely every sequence with $\mu'+\lambda'\le6$ is realised (use a path of $\mu'$ states, a cycle of $\lambda'$ states, and mark which states are in $F$; unused states are irrelevant).

Count sequences with minimal preperiod $\mu'=\mu$ and minimal period $\lambda$: the periodic part is a binary word $c$ of length $\lambda$ that is not a proper power ($f(\lambda)=\sum_{d\mid\lambda}\mu(\lambda/d)2^d$ choices: $f(1..6)=2,2,6,12,30,54$). If $\mu=0$ there is nothing else. If $\mu\ge1$, minimality of the preperiod means the last tail bit differs from the bit that periodicity would give, so it is forced, and the other $\mu-1$ tail bits are free: $2^{\mu-1}$ choices. For fixed $\lambda$ the total over $\mu=0,\dots,6-\lambda$ is $f(\lambda)(1+1+2+\dots+2^{5-\lambda})=f(\lambda)2^{6-\lambda}$.

$$\sum_{\lambda=1}^6f(\lambda)2^{6-\lambda}=2\cdot32+2\cdot16+6\cdot8+12\cdot4+30\cdot2+54\cdot1=306.$$

**Answer: 306**

cmimc-2020-combinatorics-10.title: Inclusion-exclusion over split points
cmimc-2020-combinatorics-10.body:
A string can be split after $i$ letters, $1\le i\le8$. A palindrome of length $\ell$ is determined by its first $\lceil\ell/2\rceil$ letters, so there are $4^{\lceil i/2\rceil+\lceil(9-i)/2\rceil}=4^5$ strings splittable at a given $i$ (exactly one of $i$, $9-i$ is odd, so the sum of ceilings is $5$). Summing over $i$ gives $8\cdot1024=8192$, which counts a string once per valid split point.

*Strings with two split points.* If $s=xyz$ with $x,\ yz$ palindromes and $xy,\ z$ palindromes (splits after $|x|$ and after $|xy|$), then, writing $v'$ for the reverse, $zxy=z(y'x')=(z'y')x'=\ (yz)x=yzx$, using $x=x'$, $z=z'$, $xy=y'x'$, $yz=z'y'$. So two different cyclic shifts of $s$ coincide, hence a non-trivial rotation fixes $s$. As $|s|=9$, this means $s=ttt$ with $|t|=3$.

For $s=ttt$ the number of valid split points is: $t=aaa$-type ($4$ strings): $8$; $t=aab$ or $abb$-type ($24$ strings): $3$ splits each (for example $aabaabaab$ splits after positions $1,4,7$); $t=aba$-type ($12$ strings): $2$ splits; $t$ with three different letters ($24$ strings): $0$ splits. (A direct enumeration of the $64$ strings $ttt$ gives $4$ strings with $8$ splits, $24$ with $3$, $12$ with $2$, $24$ with $0$.)

The total overcount is $\sum(\text{splits}-1)=4\cdot7+24\cdot2+12\cdot1=88$. Therefore the number of doubly palindromic strings is $8192-88=8104$ (confirmed by brute force over all $4^9$ strings).

**Answer: 8104**

cmimc-2020-combinatorics-11.title: Exact computation
cmimc-2020-combinatorics-11.body:
$p=2^{-2020}\sum_{k=0}^{505}\binom{2020}{k}$, so $-\log_2p=2020-\log_2\sum_{k\le505}\binom{2020}k$. The sum is dominated by its last terms: successive terms have ratio $\binom{2020}{k-1}/\binom{2020}k=\frac{k}{2021-k}\approx\frac13$ near $k=505$, so the sum is about $\frac32\binom{2020}{505}$ (exactly $1.4985\binom{2020}{505}$), with $\log_2\binom{2020}{505}\approx1633.1733$. Evaluating the sum exactly with big-integer arithmetic gives

$$-\log_2 p=386.24320380\ldots$$

So the requested form is $386.24320$. (The published answer key lists "(5.3605584085, 117)", which does not correspond to this question as printed; the value above is from an exact computation.)

**Answer: $386.24320$**
